hints: Focus on what the two conditions mean together, a branched C5 skeleton plus an OH on a carbon joined to two other carbons.
Start by listing the branched C5 carbon skeletons, the 2-methylbutane chain and the 2,2-dimethylpropane chain.
Try placing the OH in every different position on each branched skeleton and check if the C-OH carbon is secondary, then count only the unique structures.
walkthrough:
**Recall what secondary means**

A secondary alcohol has the OH group on a carbon attached to two other carbons and one hydrogen.

$$ \text{R}_2\text{CH-OH} $$

**List the branched C5 skeletons**

For $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$ as an alcohol, there are only two branched carbon backbones. The straight $\text{C}_5$ chain is not allowed here.

Skeleton 1: 2-methylbutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$

Skeleton 2: 2,2-dimethylpropane, $\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_4$

**Test Skeleton 1**

Put OH on this skeleton. $\text{3-methylbutan-2-ol}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$, has the OH carbon joined to two Cs, so it is secondary and branched. The other positions give $\text{2-methylbutan-1-ol}$ (primary), $\text{3-methylbutan-1-ol}$ (primary) and $\text{2-methylbutan-2-ol}$ (tertiary).

So this skeleton gives just 1 fitting isomer.

**Test Skeleton 2**

The $\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_4$ skeleton has one central C with no H and four identical $\text{CH}_3$ groups. Putting OH on a $\text{CH}_3$ gives $\text{2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol}$, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{OH}$, which is primary.

No secondary alcohol is possible here, so this skeleton gives 0.

**Conclude the count**

Total fitting structural isomers = 1 + 0 = 1. Remember straight chain secondary alcohols like pentan-2-ol and pentan-3-ol are excluded because the skeleton is not branched.

options.A: Correct. Only 3-methylbutan-2-ol fits both conditions. It has a branched 2-methylbutane skeleton and a secondary $\text{CH}(\text{OH})$ group. No other branched C5 secondary alcohol exists.
options.B: Incorrect. Students often count 2 as one from each branched skeleton, but the 2,2-dimethylpropane skeleton can only give a primary alcohol, not a secondary one.
options.C: Incorrect. Students often add in the straight chain secondary alcohols, pentan-2-ol and pentan-3-ol, forgetting the question specifically requires a branched skeleton.
options.D: Incorrect. Students often count all secondary and tertiary branched isomers together, for example including 2-methylbutan-2-ol, which is tertiary, not secondary.
